content:
At a rally for Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, President Donald Trump's speech was repeatedly interrupted by more than a dozen demonstrators, whom he promptly berated from the stage.

"That guy's gotta work out," Trump said as the removed demonstrator was being ejected.

Referring to another demonstrator, he said: "He was going home to find his mama... but what he doesn't know is his mama voted for Trump."

The president also baselessly claimed the demonstrators were being paid to heckle. "These are paid demonstrators, paid for by the enemies of our country," Trump said without evidence.

As he spoke and watched the demonstrators move through the crowd, his body language and facial expressions revealed a great deal.

"What's important to remember is that the venue is his home turf. This isn't a bipartisan thing... He's with his people. So he's not just removing the demonstrators, he's using them," said clinical psychologist and behavior expert Denise Dudley.

Dudley added that he employed a technique called "reframing for the audience," meaning he turned the disruption caused by the demonstrators into an opportunity to more sharply define the event for his supporters.

She said Trump created an "in-group/out-group" dynamic—a way for people to distinguish supporters from critics, even "good guys" from "bad guys."

Trump repeatedly commented on the motives and appearance of his opponents.

"He's describing the out-group to the in-group, which gets the in-group more excited... They start chanting 'USA,' so he uses this very effectively, essentially saying: 'Look at us, then look at those scary people over there. They're paid demonstrators,'" Dudley said.

"He's essentially attacking them in order to bring his own side closer together. So it's a tactic," she added.

Experts noted that Trump displayed tongue movements at certain moments, indicating irritation.

Patti Wood, a body language expert and author of *Snap: Making the Most of First Impressions, Body Language, and Charisma*, said that throughout the rally, Trump repeatedly made tongue movements that said a great deal.

At one point, "he pushed his tongue into the inside of his cheek—a gesture of irritation."

"He also made a movement called a 'tongue jut,' where he stuck his tongue out, which is a response to irritation," Wood said.

"This is one of my favorite nonverbal behaviors to see from a person in power, because it's like those big kids on the playground sticking their tongue out when they're bullying a kid who can't fight back," she said.

She noted that the movement was brief, but it was a "very primal" response.

"It's an indicator that he's feeling irritated, and he makes this movement before he launches an attack," Wood said.

"I see this all the time in perp walks... You never see it on a president in any situation, because they're the one in power. So that tells me that in some way, he doesn't feel like he's in power, and that's a pretty revealing thing," Wood said.

His clenched jaw and tightly pursed lips showed he was tense and trying to restrain himself.

"When you look at his face, you can't help but notice his lips," said behavioral scientist Abbie Maroño.

Trump made frequent, extensive mouth and lip movements while speaking and interacting with people.

Trump "does often purse his lips when he's irritated. So his baseline already has a lot of lip movement, but this was particularly exaggerated," Maroño said.

She said it was interesting that this occurred every time he tried to reframe the demonstrators' disruption.

"His lips are extremely pursed. Lip pursing is a behavior we use to almost conceal information... It's a gesture of restraint, something we do when we're trying to contain ourselves, when we're displeased or embarrassed and want to say something," Maroño said.

Wood added that lip pursing can have multiple meanings, but it typically signals disgust.

Maroño noted that his jaw was also visibly clenched. "You can see how tense and protruding it is... It's not just clenched, it's constantly pushing forward."

This showed an "extreme" degree of abnormality, Maroño said, and that he was trying to suppress irritation and frustration.

Experts said that when demonstrators were being removed, he would stop and stare at them—a "selfish move."

As some demonstrators were escorted out, Trump deliberately paused his speech and watched them being removed. This also caused everyone else to stop and watch.

"Whether you're in the live audience or watching the broadcast, it becomes 'nothing's going to happen until the demonstrators are gone,'" Dudley said.

"He just stops and stares—that forces all of us to know the demonstrators are being taken away. Even if we can't see them, we know." In a sense, this is making an example of someone. (殺雞儆猴)

"I think in some way that's the most selfish move you can make," Dudley said. She added that people came to the rally to hear Trump speak, but he stopped the entire event to stare and wait.

She said this was his way of bringing the entire rally to a halt and having everyone watch the "naughty demonstrators" being removed.

Certain head movements and mouth expressions showed that Trump was "irritated" and "exhausted" by the disruptions.

"I noticed he lifted his chin several times, and we typically only do that when we feel proud or are trying to project confidence," Maroño said.

She noted that this is why people remind themselves to keep their chin up when trying to appear confident.

"He lifted his chin multiple times, so he's trying to project confidence." But combined with his concealed irritation, Maroño added, this created an air of "combative confidence."

"He wasn't calm and composed. He was composed, but with irritation," she said.

With more than a dozen disruptions throughout the night, it's no wonder Trump was irritated—even if he didn't want the demonstrators to know they were getting to him.

"Now the election is so close, it's like a prolonged war where you started out full of drive and fighting spirit, but by the end, it's like you're in the final sprint and when you're that close to the finish line, you're completely exhausted," Maroño said.

"I'm starting to see a bit more of this in his recent public appearances, where he's starting to look a bit irritated," she added.

Wood agreed, noting that after Trump said "these are paid demonstrators," his eyes would "flash" and his mouth would form a downward arc.

"That tells me... he's feeling exhausted. His speech lacks power, and just the thought of them being there exhausts him," Wood said.

Trump's supporters also booed the demonstrators, which Wood said she believed confused Trump.

"At one point I was even thinking, was he wondering: 'Are those boos for me?' Like what happened to him at a football game," Wood said. Trump was booed at a Washington Commanders game last year.

"I think this shows that the negative rhetoric from these people got to him," Wood said.

Wood added that his pause before responding or acknowledging the situation also showed that he had to first figure out exactly what he wanted to do or say.

His instinct is to attack immediately, ignore others, or interrupt them, but "he didn't do that this time."

"In those moments of immediate attack, he wasn't like his usual self," Wood said.
